title: Books to use
hook: books bought for show are furniture; buy what you'll read (On Tranquility 9)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fortuna: Diogenes let his runaway servant go, and told Fortune there was nothing of hers left. Your line was mind your own business.

Day five hundred. Five hundred mornings, or nights, or lunch breaks. Some of you missed plenty and came back, which counts. Now picture a bookshelf, maybe yours. How many of those books have you actually read? And how many are there partly for how they look: to a guest, on a video call, to the person you hoped to become when you bought them? No shame. Seneca's Rome had the same habit, on a grander scale. In chapter nine of On Tranquility, right after money, he turns to the one expense that sounds above criticism. Books.
screen: `DAY FIVE HUNDRED.` → `HOW MANY HAVE YOU READ?` → `THE EXPENSE ABOVE CRITICISM.`

segments.voice: First, even good spending has a limit. Spending on study is the most honorable kind, Seneca says, but only within measure. What use are countless books whose owner can barely read the titles in a lifetime? A heap of books weighs on a learner; it doesn't teach. Better to give yourself to a few writers than to wander among many. Second, the great fire. Seneca brings up the library at Alexandria, where, he says, forty thousand books burned. The historian Livy had called it a splendid monument to the taste and care of kings. Seneca disagrees. It wasn't taste or care. It was studiosa luxuria, learned luxury. Then he takes even that back: not learned, since it was gathered for show, not for study. Third, books as furniture. He describes rich Romans who couldn't read well, their dining rooms lined with shelves to the ceiling, the book rolls valued for their handsome cases and labels. Among the baths and fine furniture, a library had become one more thing a house was expected to have. Fourth, the point for us. Seneca isn't against books; he wrote shelves of them. He's against the gap between having and using, which by now you'll recognize: rich in enough, under the gold, mind the gap. A book you read twice is worth more to you than fifty you own.
screen: `EVEN STUDY SPENDING NEEDS MEASURE.` · `ALEXANDRIA: LEARNED LUXURY.` · `SHELVES TO THE DINING-ROOM CEILING.` · `HAVING VERSUS USING.` · then, large: `READ, DON'T DISPLAY.`

segments.voice: Picture your shelf, your e-reader or your saved articles, and find one book you bought for a real reason and never opened. Remember what you hoped it would give you. Then picture opening it, the first page, the chair, the light, not to finish it, just to use it, like a tool you finally picked up.
Studiosa luxuria. Latin for learned luxury: Seneca's verdict on books gathered for show, even at Alexandria. Give yourself to a few, and read them. Today's word.
Your line: read, don't display. A shelf is a toolbox, not a trophy case. Five hundred days, and counting.

howItsDone: Readers following Seneca sometimes read a few books deeply instead of collecting many, and choose books for use rather than display.

chat.meaning: Seneca praises study within measure. Books gathered for show are learned luxury; better to give yourself to a few writers and use them.
